column5: Front-wheel-drive based; a wet multi-plate clutch on the rear axle is pre-charged by an electric pump and clamps to send torque rearward the instant slip is predicted. VAG badges it quattro / 4MOTION / 4x4 / 4Drive; Volvo uses the BorgWarner successor.
column6: Reliable if serviced. Classic failure is the Haldex pump and its filter clogging with clutch debris, dropping rear drive and throwing an AWD warning; clutch-pack wear follows on neglected cars.
column7: Haldex oil + pump filter every ~40-60k km. The most-skipped service and the main reason these fail - not 'lifetime'.

column5: Same electric-pump-and-clutch principle as Gen 5 but an earlier, slower-reacting pre-MQB generation.
column6: Same pump/filter clogging as Gen 5 but more prone to it; accumulator and pump failures on neglected cars.
column7: Haldex oil + filter every ~40-50k km; the older generation punishes neglect harder.

column5: FWD-based; wet multi-plate clutch on the rear axle. Uses a mechanical hydraulic pump that requires a speed difference (wheel slip) between front and rear axles to generate pressure and engage the clutch. Slower reacting than Gen 4/5. Used on VAG transverse 4x4/4MOTION of the mid-2000s (Octavia II pre-facelift, etc.).
column6: Mechanically robust if oil and filter are changed strictly every 60,000 km. Neglect leads to clogged filters, mechanical pump failure, and clutch-pack wear - resulting in a complete loss of AWD. Simpler and slower-reacting than the later electronic-pump generations.
column7: Haldex oil + filter change ~every 60k km, ~EUR 80-150. The single most important service for this system; the mechanical pump and filter clog and the rear clutch wears if it's skipped, causing loss of AWD.

column5: Purely mechanical torque-sensing centre differential, always engaged, shuffling torque to whichever axle has grip - no clutches or electronics in the split. RS models add an active sport rear diff.
column6: Very robust. At high km you see centre-diff and prop-shaft support-bearing wear and CV-joint wear rather than the diff itself failing.
column7: Centre and final-drive oil every ~90-120k km; otherwise almost nothing to schedule.

column5: Longitudinal but runs front-drive for economy; a clutch pack plus a dog clutch fully decouple the rear prop-shaft, then re-engage predictively before slip. Which cars got ultra vs the Torsen diff is engine-dependent.
column6: Newer with few chronic issues; watch the rear decoupler / clutch actuator and its software.
column7: Clutch-pack and rear-diff fluid per schedule (~60k km) plus normal diff oil.

column5: Rear-biased; a transfer case with an electronically-controlled multi-plate clutch normally feeds the rear and pushes torque forward on slip. M xDrive adds a disconnectable rear-only mode.
column6: Signature failure is the transfer-case actuator (servo) motor - a worn actuator gear causes a clunk/vibration and AWD fault, accelerated by neglected oil.
column7: Transfer-case oil every ~60-100k km; replace the actuator if it clunks (a known repair).

column5: Front-drive UKL platform with a GKN wet multi-plate clutch on the rear axle; shared BMW xDrive / MINI ALL4 hardware.
column6: Rear coupling and power-take-off (PTU) wear; broadly reliable.
column7: PTU and rear-diff fluid every ~60k km.

column5: Front-drive with an on-demand multi-plate coupling feeding the rear axle when needed.
column6: Coupling / PTU wear; relatively few chronic problems.
column7: Transfer/coupling fluid every ~60-80k km.

column5: Permanent-feel AWD through a transfer case with a multi-plate clutch and planetary centre; AMG 4MATIC+ is fully variable with a drift mode.
column6: Transfer-case chain and bearing wear at high km; robust otherwise, though the AMG clutch wears under repeated launches.
column7: Transfer-case and diff oil every ~60-100k km.

column5: Longitudinal boxer layout, permanently all-wheel-drive; CVT cars split torque with an electronic multi-plate transfer clutch, manuals use a viscous centre diff.
column6: Defining risk is mismatched tyres - uneven tread or wrong sizes make the centre diff/clutch bind and fail (AWD wind-up). Viscous-coupling wear on manuals.
column7: Keep all four tyres matched in size and tread (the real maintenance item); front/rear diff and transfer fluid every ~60k km.

column5: Front-drive with an electronic multi-plate rear coupling and a driver-selectable lock mode.
column6: Coupling overheating under sustained load (towing, deep snow) and actuator issues; generally reliable.
column7: Rear-coupling/diff fluid every ~60k km.

column5: Earlier Magna on-demand coupling - the same front-based, engage-on-slip principle with less sophisticated control than HTRAC.
column6: Coupling wear and overheating if worked hard.
column7: Coupling fluid every ~60k km.

column5: Predictive electronic coupling that pre-engages using sensor data (temperature, wipers, steering); front-based, except the CX-60 which is longitudinal and rear-biased.
column6: Coupling wear; few chronic issues.
column7: Transfer/coupling and diff fluid every ~60k km.

column5: Rear-biased longitudinal AWD with an actively-managed multi-plate clutch shifting torque forward.
column6: Transfer-case and actuator wear; robust but service-sensitive.
column7: Transfer-case and diff oil every ~60-90k km.

column5: Front-drive with an on-demand clutch that fully disconnects the rear axle for economy and re-engages on demand.
column6: Rear drive unit and PTU/disconnect are known trouble spots on Evoque/Discovery Sport - PTU failures common if the fluid is never changed.
column7: PTU and rear-drive-unit oil every ~45-60k km - JLR's most-neglected fluid, and skipping it is what kills these.

column5: Rear-biased longitudinal AWD with an electronically-controlled multi-plate clutch.
column6: Transfer-case and driveline wear; moderate reliability.
column7: Transfer-case and diff oil every ~60k km.

column5: PART-TIME, driver-selected 4WD (2H/4H/4L) through a transfer case with low range; NO centre differential, so 4WD must NOT be used on dry tarmac (causes driveline wind-up). Default is rear-wheel-drive.
column6: Transfer-case actuator/motor, auto-locking front-hub actuators, CV joints, and driveline damage from tarmac misuse.
column7: Transfer-case oil plus front and rear diff oil every ~40-60k km; engage 4WD briefly now and then to keep seals and actuators alive.

column5: Full-time 4WD with a locking centre differential, a 2-speed transfer case, and often front/rear diff locks - usable on any surface.
column6: Centre diff, transfer case and diff-lock actuators; on the Land Rovers the adjacent air suspension is a frequent expense.
column7: Transfer-case oil plus all diff oils (centre/front/rear) every ~40-60k km; exercise the diff locks periodically so actuators don't seize.

column5: Light on-demand coupling (Haldex-type or GKN), front-drive until slip; tuned for road and light conditions, not sustained off-road or towing load.
column6: Coupling and rear-diff overheating if towed or worked hard; coupling wear. Ford's PTU is a weak point on the Kuga family.
column7: Coupling/rear-diff fluid every ~60k km; avoid heavy towing or extended off-road that cooks the coupling.

column5: Twin-clutch rear axle with a clutch per rear wheel; can overspeed the outer rear wheel to rotate the car and send up to ~70% rear.
column6: Rear drive unit overheats and its clutches wear under track use; fluid degrades fast. (The RS head-gasket issue is an engine matter, not the drivetrain.)
column7: Rear-drive-unit (Twinster) fluid every ~30-40k km, sooner with track use - small volume, critical, routinely skipped.

column5: No propshaft - a dedicated electric motor drives the rear axle while engine/motor drive the front, with active torque vectoring across the car.
column6: Issues are hybrid/motor electronics rather than mechanical; the drive units themselves are simple.
column7: Reduction-gear/diff fluid every ~60-100k km, plus hybrid-system coolant and checks on the PHEV schedule.

column5: Separate front and rear electric motors with no mechanical link; the car splits torque in software, instantly and continuously. Nissan brands it e-4ORCE.
column6: Effectively no mechanical drivetrain wear - occasional reduction-gear whine; any real cost is motor/inverter electronics, not gears.
column7: Reduction-gear oil is usually genuine lifetime (change only ~100-150k km where a maker specifies it); the scheduled item is motor/inverter/battery coolant per the maker's interval.

column5: No propshaft; the front axle is driven by a hybrid combustion powertrain while the rear axle is driven entirely by a separate, independent electric motor (e.g., Toyota E-Four or Nissan e-POWER).
column6: Highly reliable due to the lack of mechanical AWD components (transfer case or propshaft). AWD performance is strictly bound by battery charge; prolonged heavy load can deplete the battery and temporarily disable rear drive.
column7: Rear reduction-gear/differential fluid every ~60-100k km, alongside regular hybrid-system coolant checks.
